title: Being loved
hookLine: receiving love is part of holiness too
tomorrow: what can happen in the five minutes before Mass even starts?

cards: Someone offers to pay, and you're already reaching for your card. Someone asks how you are, and you say fine and turn the question around. Being on the receiving end takes practice.
At the Last Supper, Jesus takes off his outer garment, ties a towel around himself, pours water into a basin and starts washing his friends' feet. When he reaches Peter, Peter stops him.
In the Douay-Rheims Bible: "Thou shalt never wash my feet."

teach.b: So why refuse? Peter can't bear to see his teacher kneeling at his dusty feet. It sounds like humility.
Jesus answers: "If I wash thee not, thou shalt have no part with me." Being loved isn't optional; it's the way in. So Peter swings the other way: not only my feet, but my hands and my head.
Then Jesus says that once they've been served, they're to do the same for one another. Receiving comes first.
John's first letter puts the order plainly: "Let us therefore love God, because God first hath loved us." A neighbor tradition knows this lesson by heart.
In Jewish practice, after a burial, mourners sitting shiva don't make their own first meal.

Neighbors bring it, the meal of condolence, called the seudat havra'ah, and the Talmud and later Jewish law say the mourner shouldn't eat his own bread at that meal. The mourner's part, for once, is simply to be fed.
That's shared ground: both traditions count receiving care as part of a holy life, not a failure at it.
And an honest difference: Catholics see the deepest picture in Jesus, whom they believe is God made flesh, kneeling at Peter's feet.
Judaism doesn't hold that God took flesh; its meal is a commandment neighbors keep for one another.

how: On Holy Thursday, at the Mass of the Lord's Supper, the priest may wash the feet of members of the congregation, re-enacting John 13.

o: letting yourself receive care without earning it
being admired and praised by the people around you
loving others so they'll love you back in turn

p: thou shalt never wash my feet

s: Jesus praised Peter's humility for refusing the foot washing
he said: if I wash thee not, thou shalt have no part with me.
in Jewish practice, mourners cook the first meal after a burial for their guests
neighbors bring it, the meal of condolence. the mourner's part is to be fed.
John's first letter says God loved us first

games.q: you visit a friend's family sitting shiva, carrying food. her mom gets up to serve you. what fits the custom you just heard?
o: gently ask her to sit, and let the visitors do the serving.
let her serve you; refusing a host would be rude.
leave the food at the door and go home quickly.
games.why: mourners don't make their own first meal; neighbors bring it. at a shiva house, the family is on the receiving end.

practice: Find one thing near you that someone else made, gave or fixed for you: a mug, a sweater, a note, the meal you just ate.
Hold it or look at it for a while, and let yourself stay on the receiving end, without planning how to pay it back. If you pray, you can give thanks for the person behind it.

wordCard.voice: Being loved. Letting yourself receive care, from God and from people, without earning it first. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: I wash. Jesus to Peter in John 13:8: if I wash thee not.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: let yourself be loved, the way Peter finally held out his feet. That's the day, and the week is nearly done.
